addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

# Todo

This file uses [Prose form](AGENTS.md#prose-form). It contains near term tasks with a short
description and uses links or reference links for more details.

## In Progress

When a `## Todo` item is picked up, its text moves here: the problem overview and its list of
things to do. That is followed by the "plan", a bulleted list of the development "ladder":
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-0 blah (done)
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-1 blah blah (current)
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-2 blah blah blah
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y close-out and validation

**feat: measure reproducibility**

No report this project has produced records the machine's power policy, and no run's numbers
survive the session that produced them. The 2026-08-03 pinning experiment paid both costs at
once: a policy delta that cannot be separated from box history, and a powersave series that
exists only in a transcript because the rerun overwrote its files. This cycle makes a run
self-describing (the policy on the display, one machine-readable record per run on disk), then
reruns the pinning experiment on 3900X, 7600x, and rpi5-20cd.

What the harness is for, stated here because it decides calls like the ones below and is written
down nowhere in the repo (wink, 2026-08-04): **A/B comparison of algorithm changes**, did this
change make it faster or slower. It deserves a permanent home in the README's overview; the cycle
block is where it landed first.

- the far tail is a validity check, not the score: beyond ~n4 on a 20 ns operation it measures OS
  interruptions (context switches, IRQs, faults, migrations), so it says whether to trust a
  comparison, never whether the algorithm improved
- the near tail is not in that bucket: cache miss rates, a ring's wrap boundary and the 2t benches'
  producer/consumer phase relationships live around p99, and a change that improves the median
  while doubling p99 is usually a worse algorithm
- a comparison needs a resolution claim, not just a number, which is what makes rung -4
  load-bearing rather than last: an A/B verdict is only as good as the smallest delta the tool can
  honestly distinguish

Carried from the Todo entry, the measurement that motivates the cycle (measured 2026-08-03; the
session's terminal stamps read 26-08-04 UTC):

- the measurement: `min-now --blocks 200`, 8 pinned + 8 unpinned per policy, alternating so box
  history is shared between conditions, under amd-pstate-epp `powersave` then `performance`
  - powersave unpinned: 23.927 ns, run-to-run stdev 0.785 ns (3.28%), grades 4 A / 2 D / 2 F
  - powersave pinned to one core: 22.207 ns, 0.073 ns (0.33%), all 8 graded D
  - performance unpinned: 21.980 ns, 0.057 ns (0.26%), no D or F in 17 runs
  - performance pinned: 22.359 ns, 0.311 ns (1.39%)
  - what that supports, and how strongly:
    - the policy delta is big and one-directional: 8.9% on the unpinned mean, with unpinned
      run-to-run scatter falling from 0.785 ns to 0.057 ns
    - but policy could not be alternated the way pinning was (setting EPP needs root and is
      global and persistent), so the two policies are separated in time and the delta is
      confounded with box history exactly as the `--blocks` sweep was. We think an effect this
      size survives de-confounding, but this experiment does not show it
    - pinning under powersave is the strongest result here: 7.2% off the mean and 10x off the
      scatter, on alternated runs
    - pinning under performance is the weakest: 1.7% *worse* than unpinned, and the whole gap is
      four consecutive pinned runs (p3-p6) at 22.59-22.70 ns while the pinned runs on either side
      sat at 22.08-22.09 ns and the unpinned runs interleaved with them did not move. So the
      0.311 ns is the width of a state change, not scatter about a mean

content.content:
60	      0.311 ns is the width of a state change, not scatter about a mean
61	    - the pinning answer therefore looks policy-dependent, but "pinning loses under performance"
62	      rests on that one cluster and should be treated as unreproduced
63	- the finding that reframes the grade: A was being awarded to the un-boosted floor. A powersave A
64	  run puts ~73% of its samples on 23.967 ns, the 3.7929 GHz TSC/base rate, while the boosted
65	  states are 21.79 / 22.22. Flatness is all the grade sees, and base clock is the flattest place
66	  on the box
67	- rung -2's spec: move the report renderer out of `harness.rs` into its own module, a pure move
68	  plus the `_w` -> `_cols` rename that already landed in -1
69	  - `harness.rs` is ~2,500 lines carrying the `Bench` trait, the warm loop, sizing, the batch
70	    pipeline, the run loop *and* ~350 lines of renderer, which shares nothing with the measuring
71	    code except the value it reads
72	  - the seam already exists: `RunOutput` is what `print_report` takes. What is missing is a
73	    module boundary, not a design
74	  - it goes *before* the record and not after, so -3's diff reads as "add the record" rather than
75	    "move 350 lines and add the record". The record is also what makes the split honest: today
76	    `RunOutput` has one consumer, so "what belongs in the model" is whatever the printer needs,
77	    and two consumers is what forces a real answer
78	  - visible from there, not folded in: `band_table.rs` renders a band table for `tprobe` /
79	    `tprobe2` with the same shape as `print_report`'s, so the project has two band-table
80	    renderers. Its own cleanup, once they are in one place
81	- rung -4's spec: `qualify-environment` reads the policy as a fitness precondition and says so
82	  before spending minutes on numbers it can predict will scatter
83	  - a diagnosis, never a mutation: setting the governor needs root and is global and persistent,
84	    and the 2026-08-03 session's documented revert left EPP at `performance` after the governor
85	    had already returned to `powersave`
86	- rung -5's spec, the cycle's most valuable rung given the A/B purpose above: LSC is scoped to
87	  within-run block agreement but reads as a run-to-run bound
88	  - the best configuration printed LSC 0.022 ns against a measured run-to-run stdev of 0.057 ns,
89	    so single-run against single-run resolution is ~0.157 ns (0.71%) where the report prints
90	    0.10%
91	  - about 7x optimistic, and it did not improve when the environment did
92	  - the fix is a **variance-versus-aggregation curve**, not a second measurement: a single run
93	    runs once, so it cannot measure run-to-run scatter directly. Aggregate its blocks in groups
94	    of 1, 2, 4, 8, ... and watch whether variance falls as `1/n`. Where it stops falling is the
95	    drift floor, and that floor is the run's honest resolution
96	    - this is Allan deviation (IEEE Std 1139), the standard tool in clock metrology for "how
97	      long should I average"; the harness is already a clock project, so the machinery is
98	      familiar rather than exotic
99	    - the alternative, spawning children as `qualify-environment` does, is a much larger change
100	      and still cannot re-roll thermal or P-state history, so it does not actually reach the
101	      component we are missing
102	    - the duration estimate falls out of the same curve for free:
103	      `t_needed = t_now * (SE_now / SE_target)^2`, valid only in the region where the `1/n`
104	      scaling still holds, which the curve is what tells us
105	    - naming it accurately matters as much as computing it: a within-run bound must not print in
106	      a way that reads as a run-to-run one, which is the whole defect
107	- evidence is perishable: `tmp/pinexp/` holds only the performance series (the rerun overwrote
108	  powersave), so the powersave numbers live only in the session transcript until copied into a
109	  chores design subsection

0.311 ns is the width of a state change, not scatter about a mean
    - the pinning answer therefore looks policy-dependent, but "pinning loses under performance"
      rests on that one cluster and should be treated as unreproduced
- the finding that reframes the grade: A was being awarded to the un-boosted floor. A powersave A
  run puts ~73% of its samples on 23.967 ns, the 3.7929 GHz TSC/base rate, while the boosted
  states are 21.79 / 22.22. Flatness is all the grade sees, and base clock is the flattest place
  on the box
- rung -2's spec: move the report renderer out of `harness.rs` into its own module, a pure move
  plus the `_w` -> `_cols` rename that already landed in -1
  - `harness.rs` is ~2,500 lines carrying the `Bench` trait, the warm loop, sizing, the batch
    pipeline, the run loop *and* ~350 lines of renderer, which shares nothing with the measuring
    code except the value it reads
  - the seam already exists: `RunOutput` is what `print_report` takes. What is missing is a
    module boundary, not a design
  - it goes *before* the record and not after, so -3's diff reads as "add the record" rather than
    "move 350 lines and add the record". The record is also what makes the split honest: today
    `RunOutput` has one consumer, so "what belongs in the model" is whatever the printer needs,
    and two consumers is what forces a real answer
  - visible from there, not folded in: `band_table.rs` renders a band table for `tprobe` /
    `tprobe2` with the same shape as `print_report`'s, so the project has two band-table
    renderers. Its own cleanup, once they are in one place
- rung -4's spec: `qualify-environment` reads the policy as a fitness precondition and says so
  before spending minutes on numbers it can predict will scatter
  - a diagnosis, never a mutation: setting the governor needs root and is global and persistent,
    and the 2026-08-03 session's documented revert left EPP at `performance` after the governor
    had already returned to `powersave`
- rung -5's spec, the cycle's most valuable rung given the A/B purpose above: LSC is scoped to
  within-run block agreement but reads as a run-to-run bound
  - the best configuration printed LSC 0.022 ns against a measured run-to-run stdev of 0.057 ns,
    so single-run against single-run resolution is ~0.157 ns (0.71%) where the report prints
    0.10%
  - about 7x optimistic, and it did not improve when the environment did
  - the fix is a **variance-versus-aggregation curve**, not a second measurement: a single run
    runs once, so it cannot measure run-to-run scatter directly. Aggregate its blocks in groups
    of 1, 2, 4, 8, ... and watch whether variance falls as `1/n`. Where it stops falling is the
    drift floor, and that floor is the run's honest resolution
    - this is Allan deviation (IEEE Std 1139), the standard tool in clock metrology for "how
      long should I average"; the harness is already a clock project, so the machinery is
      familiar rather than exotic
    - the alternative, spawning children as `qualify-environment` does, is a much larger change
      and still cannot re-roll thermal or P-state history, so it does not actually reach the
      component we are missing
    - the duration estimate falls out of the same curve for free:
      `t_needed = t_now * (SE_now / SE_target)^2`, valid only in the region where the `1/n`
      scaling still holds, which the curve is what tells us
    - naming it accurately matters as much as computing it: a within-run bound must not print in
      a way that reads as a run-to-run one, which is the whole defect

Your reasoning is sound, and I tried it rather than guessing. Results:

## What happened

Both musl targets are already installed. `cargo build --release --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl` gets through the entire tree except one crate:

```
error[E0425]: cannot find function `pthread_attr_setaffinity_np` in crate `libc`
error[E0425]: cannot find function `pthread_rwlockattr_setkind_np` in crate `libc`
error: could not compile `iceoryx2-pal-posix` (lib)
```

Those are genuine musl gaps, not libc-crate oversights: both are glibc extensions musl does not implement. Nothing else in the tree failed.

iceoryx2 is confined to four bench files (`ice_ps_1t`, `ice_ps_2t`, `ice_rr_1t`, `ice_rr_2t`), so a cargo feature gate is a small, clean change. But it means the portable build ships without the iceoryx benches, and inter-application communication is in the crate's own description. That is a real cost, not a footnote.

## The substantive objection

`src/benches/min_now.rs` benches `std::time::Instant::now()`, which is libc's `clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC)` through the vDSO. The flagship bench measures libc. Switching libc does not just change how the harness is built, it changes what that bench measures, and every number on record (the 2026-08-03 pinning experiment, the grades, the quantum work that landed in -1) is a glibc number. That lands in the middle of a cycle whose whole subject is reproducibility.

Two risks follow:

- musl does use the vDSO for `clock_gettime` on x86_64 and aarch64, but if that lookup ever falls back to a real syscall, `min-now` goes from ~22 ns to a few hundred. Cheap to detect: one run tells us.
- musl's mallocng is slower and more contended than glibc malloc, and its pthread/futex behavior differs. That would show in the 2t benches, not in `min-now`.

Things I checked that are *not* risks: `sched_getcpu` is called once per run in `freq.rs:41` plus test paths, so glibc's rseq fast path versus musl's syscall does not matter here. `sched_getaffinity` and `CLOCK_BOOTTIME` are also once per run. And static linking is a genuine measurement *benefit*: no PLT indirection, no ld.so startup variance.

One cheaper alternative worth naming since you asked for reasons not to: if the goal is only "runs on the Pi's older glibc", building the gnu target in an old-glibc container keeps glibc semantics and keeps iceoryx2, at zero measurement change. (`+crt-static` on the gnu target is not a real option: static glibc is discouraged and breaks NSS.)

## Recommendation

Do it, but not before -3, and split it:

1. **In -3, record the target triple and libc flavor.** That is exactly what "self-describing" means, it costs almost nothing, and it meets the cycle's own stated test: cheap now, impossible to backfill.
2. **Make the musl switch its own cycle after 0.25.0 closes.** It is architecture-shaped (feature-gating a dependency, a second build target), so by the project's scope rule it wants a minor bump of its own rather than a rung inside this one.
3. **Validate the port with the harness.** First run after switching is `min-now` glibc-versus-musl, same box, same session, alternated. This tool exists to answer "did this change make it faster or slower", and the port is a change.

The open question is the three-box rerun that sits between -3 and -4. If we switch afterwards, that series is glibc evidence and a later switch invalidates its absolute numbers, though its within-box pinned-versus-unpinned conclusions survive. If that bothers you, the switch moves ahead of the rerun instead, and -3 grows a feature gate.

**The plain version:** nothing stops us technically except iceoryx2, which we can gate off in a few lines. The real catch is that our headline benchmark measures libc itself, so changing libc changes the thing we are measuring, right in the cycle about making measurements reproducible. So: record the libc in -3 now, switch to musl as its own cycle right after, and let the harness measure its own port.

Which way do you want the rerun to fall, before or after the switch?

content.text:
Checked, and the answer is better than I gave you, but not via the glibc route.

## Don't copy glibc's code

Those two are not portable algorithms, they are glibc-internal wiring:

- `pthread_attr_setaffinity_np` writes a cpuset into glibc's `struct pthread_attr`, and glibc's `pthread_create` reads it back at thread start. Copy that code onto musl and it scribbles into a `pthread_attr_t` that musl's `pthread_create` never consults. It would compile, link, and silently do nothing.
- `pthread_rwlockattr_setkind_np` sets a preference flag that glibc's rwlock algorithm honors. musl's rwlock is a different algorithm with no such knob, so "porting" it means reimplementing musl's rwlock, not copying a function.

Also glibc is LGPL-2.1 and iceoryx2 is MIT OR Apache-2.0 (verified in its `Cargo.toml`), so copying would relicense a dependency.

## The right route is already built into iceoryx2

`iceoryx2-pal-posix/src/` has seven platform modules: `android`, `freebsd`, `linux`, `macos`, `qnx`, `stub`, `windows`. Adding `musl` beside `linux` is the crate's own extension point. And Android and QNX already ship exactly the two shims we need: a no-op `rwlockattr_setkind_np` returning 0, and a stubbed `attr_setaffinity_np` (Android's even prints a TODO).

So you were right that it isn't hard. It is a new platform module, not a libc port.

## And the shims are inert for us

This is the part that decides it. I traced both functions through the whole iceoryx2 tree:

- `pthread_rwlockattr_setkind_np`: **zero callers anywhere.** It is unused PAL surface, defined on every platform and invoked by none.
- `pthread_attr_setaffinity_np`: exactly one caller, `iceoryx2-bb-posix/src/thread.rs:510`, in iceoryx2's own `ThreadBuilder`. Nothing in our `src/` touches `iceoryx2_bb_posix` or `ThreadBuilder`. Our four ice benches use `std::thread::spawn` and pin through our own `pin.rs` / `cfg.core_for(1)`.

So a musl PAL is not "degraded iceoryx2 with a documented caveat". Both shims sit on paths our benches never execute. That was my main worry and it does not apply.

(0.9.3 is out and is already in the local cache, still calling the same thing at `thread.rs:510`, so upgrading does not fix it for free.)

## On benching either libc

Agreed, that is the strongest part of the idea, and worth separating from the iceoryx work: there are 17 bench files, 4 of them iceoryx. A feature gate alone gives us both-libc benching on 13 benches today at the cost of a few lines. The PAL module buys the remaining 4. So the gate is worth doing first regardless, it is the prerequisite either way, and it is most of the value.

The one cost that survives: we run a `[patch.crates-io]` fork until upstream takes the module. For a measurement harness that normally means "these numbers describe our fork", which is why the inert-shim finding matters so much. Given MIT/Apache and the existing platform pattern, upstreaming looks like a small, welcome PR.

## Revised recommendation

1. **-3 as planned**, plus target triple and libc flavor as record fields. Unchanged advice, and now it earns more since a run really can be either.
2. **New cycle after 0.25.0 closes: "build and bench on musl and glibc."** Feature-gate iceoryx, add the musl PAL module, upstream it, then A/B the two libcs with the harness itself. That is architecture-shaped, so minor bump, which is the right home for it.

**The plain version:** your instinct was right that the two functions are easy, but wrong about where the code comes from. We do not port glibc, we add a musl platform module to iceoryx2 the way it already has Android and QNX ones, with a no-op and a stub. And it turns out neither function is ever called on any path our benches use, so nothing is silently degraded. Meanwhile 13 of our 17 benches build on musl right now with just a feature gate.

Still open from before: do you want the three-box rerun before or after the libc switch?

content.text:
Yes, it means modifying iceoryx2's source. There is no way to do it from outside: the failing line is `libc::pthread_attr_setaffinity_np` *inside* their crate, and Rust has no mechanism to inject items into another crate's namespace.

But the diff is smaller than I said. I was wrong about "a musl platform module": the PAL selects platforms by `target_os`, and musl is `target_os = "linux"`, so musl already routes through `src/linux/`. There is no new platform to add. The fix is a `#[cfg(target_env = "musl")]` branch inside `src/linux/pthread.rs` around two functions, roughly 10 to 15 lines, using the Android/QNX shims as the model.

## How to carry the patch

Three ways, all of which involve our own copy of that crate:

1. **Fork on GitHub, `[patch.crates-io]` to it.** Patch only `iceoryx2-pal-posix`; `iceoryx2` and `iceoryx2-bb-posix` still come from crates.io, and resolution works as long as the fork keeps version 0.9.2. This matches what you already do with `zc-ring-x1 = { git = "https://github.com/winksaville/zc-ring-x1" }`.
2. **Vendor it locally**, `[patch.crates-io] iceoryx2-pal-posix = { path = "vendor/..." }`. The diff lives in our own history, which is good for provenance, but it drags about 2,000 lines of someone else's code into the harness repo.
3. **Upstream PR**, which is the durable answer. Small diff, follows their existing precedent, MIT or Apache-2.0. We still need 1 or 2 while it is in flight.

I would do 1 plus 3: fork, patch, open the PR, drop the patch when it lands.

## The one route that avoids touching iceoryx2

Patch the `libc` crate instead, adding the two declarations under musl. It compiles, then fails at **link** time, because musl genuinely does not export those symbols. So we would also need `#[no_mangle] extern "C"` definitions in our own binary to satisfy the linker. It works, but it trades a small stable crate for `libc`, which churns constantly, and it puts us in the business of defining libc-namespace symbols inside a benchmarking binary. Not worth it.

## Worth keeping in view

The genuinely zero-fork option is still the feature gate: 13 of 17 benches on musl, no third-party code modified at all. The fork is the price of the 4 iceoryx benches specifically. That is a real payoff, since IIAC is the crate's stated subject, but it is worth being clear that it is what we are buying.

**The plain version:** yes, we need our own copy of one iceoryx2 crate, most likely a fork on your GitHub wired in with `[patch.crates-io]`, same pattern as `zc-ring-x1`. The change itself is about a dozen lines in one file, not a new platform module, and it is a good upstream PR. If you would rather not carry a fork at all, the feature gate still gets you musl builds for 13 of the 17 benches.

aiTitle: Statically link with musl for portability

content.text:
Good news from the registry: `REGISTRY: &[(&str, RunFn)]` in `src/benches/mod.rs:30` is already a const catalog, separate from the `Bench` trait. That is exactly the seam this needs, so the change is smaller than it looks.

## 1. "Feature" is the wrong primitive for libc, the right one for iceoryx

Cargo features are additive, unified across the graph, and user-settable. A `musl` / `glibc` feature pair could be set to both, neither, or the one that contradicts the target triple, and nothing would catch it. In a tool whose product is trustworthy numbers, a switch that can disagree with the build is a liability.

`cfg(target_env = "musl")` is derived from the triple and cannot disagree. That is the libc primitive.

What genuinely wants to be a feature is `iceoryx`, gating the optional dependency. And it is needed in **both** directions, which is the part worth noticing: an honest musl-versus-glibc A/B wants the same bench set on both sides, so we need to build *glibc without iceoryx* too. A pure target gate would not give us that.

## 2. One mechanism question to settle first

Whether these compose:

```toml
[target.'cfg(target_env = "gnu")'.dependencies]
iceoryx2 = { version = "0.9.2", optional = true }

[features]
default = ["std", "iceoryx"]
iceoryx = ["dep:iceoryx2"]
```

If Cargo tolerates `dep:iceoryx2` when the dependency is absent for the current target, we get the ideal: musl builds just work, and glibc can still opt out for parity. I am not certain it does. Worth a five minute experiment before designing around it.

If it does not compose, the fallback is a plain optional dependency plus the feature, and musl needs `--no-default-features --features std`. One honest downside: we cannot give a forgetful musl build a nice message. `compile_error!` in our crate is never reached, because Cargo builds the dependency first, so you get the raw `E0425` out of iceoryx2's internals. The mitigation is a documented command or a `.cargo/config.toml` alias, not a code fix.

## 3. Where the declaration lives

In the registry entry, not the `Bench` trait. `Bench` is the per-workload interface (`name`, `step`), and on musl the ice types do not exist to answer the question. The catalog is the thing that must survive on every target.

```rust
pub struct BenchEntry {
    pub name: &'static str,
    pub libc: LibcSupport,   // Both | GnuOnly
    pub run: Option<RunFn>,  // None when cfg'd out of this build
}
```

The load-bearing discipline: **`libc` is target-invariant, `run.is_some()` is target-dependent.** `libc` is a property of the bench and carries the same value in every build, so the catalog is identical on musl and glibc. Availability is *derived* (`entry.libc.allows(BUILD_LIBC)`) and never stored.

That is the whole point. It means a musl record and a glibc record differ only in two recorded facts, the build's `target_env` and each bench's declared `libc`, so the coverage gap between them is computable. The alternative, cfg'ing entries out of the table, makes `list` print 13 names on one box and 17 on another with nothing in either output explaining why. In a cycle whose subject is making a run self-describing, that is the wrong answer.

On the enum: keep `Both | GnuOnly` and do not add a `MuslOnly` variant until something needs it. An enum with a speculative variant is worse than a two-state one that can grow.

## 4. Behavior that falls out

- `list` shows all 17 on both libcs, unavailable ones marked with the reason.
- `ice-ps-1t` on musl reports "requires glibc, this build is `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl`" instead of "unknown bench", which is what a cfg'd-out table would say and is actively misleading.
- `all` on musl skips the four and *says so*, and -3's record carries the skip list. Without that, a musl `all` and a glibc `all` look like the same experiment.
- The prefix rule at `mod.rs:71` (`ice` matching all four) currently falls through to "unknown bench" when nothing matches. With the catalog it can say the accurate thing.

## 5. Keeping the declaration honest

It can rot: someone cfg's a module out without touching `libc`, or the reverse. Same failure mode as -3's field dictionary, and the same remedy, which matches the taste already set there: a test asserting `entry.libc.allows(BUILD_LIBC) == entry.run.is_some()` for every entry. Run on both targets, it turns a mismatch into a build failure rather than a convention to remember.

## 6. Resist generalizing

The pull will be toward `Requirements { libc, min_cores, arch, needs_root }`. I would not, yet: libc is the only axis with a real case today, and a taxonomy invented around one member usually gets the shape wrong. Naming the field `libc` rather than something vague like `available` keeps a second axis additive later.

## 7. Sequencing

This touches every registry entry plus `names`, `resolve`, the CLI listing, and a new test. By your scope rule it is shape, not contents: the registry gains a contract. It is also independently valuable and revertable, which is the criterion that got -2 its own rung.

So I would slot it as a rung ahead of -3, `0.25.0-3 feat: benches declare their libc support`, renumbering the rest down. It makes -3's record schema right the first time rather than retrofitted, and it delivers musl builds for 13 of 17 benches with **zero** third-party changes, leaving the iceoryx2 fork decision genuinely deferred rather than implied.

**The plain version:** do not make libc a Cargo feature, it is a target property and a feature could contradict the build. Do make `iceoryx` a feature, since we need to drop it on glibc too for a fair comparison. Put the libc declaration in the existing `REGISTRY` table as a value that is the same on every target, and derive availability from it, so a musl run and a glibc run explain their own difference instead of just having one. Then it wants to be a rung before -3, not a side edit.

Two things still open: whether that Cargo composition works, and whether the three-box rerun lands before or after the libc switch.

content.text:
Checked, and one thing lands before the design question: `config.toml` is already taken. `src/config.rs:4` defines it as the user's runtime config at `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/iiac-perf/config.toml`, layered with a project-local `iiac-perf.toml`. A second, unrelated `config.toml` meaning per-bench build metadata would collide with an established concept in the same tool.

Past the name, three problems and one place the instinct is right.

## The phase is wrong

Whether `ice_ps_1t::run` exists at all is decided at compile time by `cfg`. A TOML file read at runtime cannot make a registry entry reference a function that was never compiled. So we would still need the cfg, and the TOML becomes a *second* source of truth sitting beside it, free to disagree. That is worse than one source, and it is precisely the desync that the honesty test in my last message existed to prevent.

There is a variant that does work: a `build.rs` that reads the per-bench TOMLs and generates the registry, cfgs included. Single source of truth, genuinely coherent. The costs are a build script (the project has none today), a generated registry that is harder to grep than a table you can read, and TOML parsing in the build graph. For one enum with two values, that is a lot of machinery.

## It gives back the portability we came for

If the files are read at runtime they have to ship next to the binary. The entire premise of this thread is scp'ing one self-contained static binary to the Pi. A static musl build that then needs a directory of TOML files beside it undoes that.

`include_str!` dodges it by baking them in, but then we are parsing TOML at startup to learn a fact that was known at compile time, which is a const with extra steps.

## The file layout cost is real

Benches are single files today (`src/benches/ice_ps_1t.rs`). A per-bench `config.toml` needs a per-bench directory, so all 17 become `src/benches/<name>/{mod.rs, config.toml}`. That is a repo-wide restructure in exchange for one two-valued field.

## "Absent means both" points the wrong way for this tool

Silence meaning "works everywhere" means a new bench that quietly does not work on musl looks correct until someone runs it on a Pi. Your own -3 design took the opposite position: a test that fails on any *undocumented* record key, rather than a default that fills the gap. A required field in a struct makes the compiler ask the question for every new bench, at zero cost.

## Where the instinct is right, and how to get it cheaply

Two things you are reaching for are worth having: declare it near the bench, and do not make me write `Both` thirteen times. Neither needs files.

- **Colocation**: each bench module already exposes `NAME` and `run`, so `pub const LIBC: LibcSupport` sits naturally right beside them, and the registry references `ice_ps_1t::LIBC`.
- **Defaulting**: a small `bench!` macro gives `bench!(min_now)` for `Both` and `bench!(ice_ps_1t, GnuOnly)` when it differs, and the same macro can emit the `#[cfg]`, so name, run fn, libc, and gate are one line that cannot desync.

I would still take the plain explicit field over both. At 17 entries the table is one screen, and you can read the harness's entire libc story at a glance, which a per-file scheme destroys. Thirteen rows saying `Both` is signal, not noise.

## Where it would genuinely win

If per-bench metadata grows well past this one axis, description, min cores, arch, default parameters, doc text, or if benches ever become externally contributed or discovered rather than compiled in, then per-bench manifests plus a generated registry is the right architecture. That is a real future, just not this change. Worth revisiting when the second and third fields show up.

**The plain version:** the name is already used for the user's runtime config, and the deeper issue is timing. Whether an ice bench exists is settled when the code compiles, so a runtime TOML cannot decide it and would only add a second thing to keep in sync. It would also make the binary need files beside it, which is the opposite of why we want musl, and it would turn all 17 bench files into directories. What you actually want, declared near the bench and defaulting to both, is available as a const in each module plus a small macro. My recommendation stays the explicit field in the existing table, but tell me if you would rather have the macro and I will spec that instead.

# Design note: per-bench glibc/musl support in iiac-perf

## Problem

We want to compare benches built against glibc vs musl. Each bench is a
single file implementing the `Bench` trait:

```rust
pub trait Bench {
    /// Human-readable name used in the report header.
    fn name(&self) -> &str;
    /// Run one unit of work. Return any value derived from the work
    /// to defeat DCE — the caller black-boxes it.
    fn step(&mut self) -> u64;
}
```

Original idea: a `const fn` on the trait that "detects" glibc/musl/both.

## Key reframe

The libc is a **whole-binary, compile-time property** baked into the target
triple (`x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` vs `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl`). There is
nothing to detect per-bench at runtime, and a single binary is never "both."

What we actually need:

1. Each bench **declares** which libc environments it is meaningful on.
2. The harness knows what it was **built against** and filters/annotates.
3. The comparison workflow is a **build matrix**: compile twice, run both
   binaries, diff the reports.

## Harness: what was this binary built against?

`cfg!` works in const context:

```rust
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Debug)]
pub enum Libc { Glibc, Musl, Other }

pub const TARGET_LIBC: Libc = if cfg!(target_env = "gnu") {
    Libc::Glibc
} else if cfg!(target_env = "musl") {
    Libc::Musl
} else {
    Libc::Other
};
```

## Bench declaration: default trait method, not associated const

Benches are registered as `Box<dyn Bench>`. An associated const breaks dyn
compatibility, and `const fn` in traits is unstable. Use a
default-implemented method — dyn-safe, and benches that run everywhere
don't need to touch it:

```rust
pub trait Bench {
    fn name(&self) -> &str;
    fn step(&mut self) -> u64;

    /// Which libc environments this bench is meaningful on. Default: all.
    fn supports(&self, libc: Libc) -> bool {
        let _ = libc;
        true
    }
}
```

Harness behavior:

```rust
if !bench.supports(TARGET_LIBC) {
    // record as SKIPPED in the report — do NOT silently drop it
}
```

Recording skips (rather than omitting) keeps the bench roster identical
between a glibc report and a musl report, so the two reports are diffable
line-for-line.

## Benches that won't even compile on one libc

If a bench uses glibc-only APIs (e.g. `gnu_get_libc_version`, glibc malloc
internals), declaration isn't enough — gate it at compile time so it never
enters the registry:

```rust
#[cfg(target_env = "gnu")]
mod glibc_malloc_probe;
```

The two mechanisms compose: `#[cfg]` for "won't build", `supports()` for
"builds but not meaningful."

## Report header

Stamp every report with:

- `TARGET_LIBC` and the full target triple
- On glibc, the runtime version via `gnu_get_libc_version()` (musl
  deliberately has no version API)

## Methodology caveat: allocator, not libc

musl's mallocng allocator is dramatically slower than glibc's malloc,
especially under threads. Any bench that allocates on the hot path will
measure **allocators**, not libc syscall wrappers or startup behavior.

Mitigation: add a run variant with `#[global_allocator]` pinned to
mimalloc or jemalloc on *both* targets, so the reported libc delta is the
delta we think it is. (zcr-mpsc benches are allocation-free by design, so
this mainly matters for future benches.)

## Build matrix

```sh
cargo build --release --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
cargo build --release --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl
# run both, diff reports
```

Same applies to aarch64 targets (`aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` /
`aarch64-unknown-linux-musl`) for the Graviton/Altra/Pi 5 deployments.

content.text:
Read it. It converges with where we landed on the principles, contributes two things I did not, and has one structural error that happens to break on exactly the four benches that started this.

## What it gets right, including two improvements on my version

- The reframe is correct and matches: libc is a whole-binary compile-time property, nothing to detect per bench, a binary is never "both."
- Skip-and-record rather than drop, so the two reports stay diffable line for line. Same conclusion as the target-invariant catalog, better stated.
- **The two-mechanism split is a genuine refinement.** `#[cfg]` for "won't build" versus a declaration for "builds but is not meaningful" are different facts, and I had collapsed them into one. That is the better model.
- `gnu_get_libc_version()` in the report header, with the note that musl deliberately has none, is a good concrete detail I did not offer.
- The allocator mitigation (pin the same allocator on both targets as a run variant) is a real improvement on my raising mallocng without a remedy.
- `TARGET_LIBC` via `cfg!` in const position does work as written.

## The structural error

The note says "Benches are registered as `Box<dyn Bench>`." They are not. There is no `dyn Bench` anywhere in the tree, and no boxing. `src/benches/mod.rs:30` is:

```rust
pub const REGISTRY: &[(&str, RunFn)]   // RunFn = fn(&RunCfg)
```

Plain function pointers. `Bench` is a per-workload interface used generically inside each bench's own `run`, implemented by 14 concrete types and monomorphized. So the whole chain of reasoning ("associated const breaks dyn compatibility, therefore default trait method") is answering a constraint we do not have.

That matters beyond tidiness. `fn supports(&self, libc) -> bool` needs **an instance** of the bench to ask. On musl the four iceoryx types do not compile at all, so there is no instance to construct and no one to ask. The declaration has to survive the bench not existing, and a method on the bench cannot. It fails precisely on the case that motivated the exercise.

Related smaller smell: `supports(&self, libc: Libc)` takes a libc parameter, but the note argues two sections earlier that a binary only ever has one. The parameter is dead on arrival.

## What it misses

It never mentions iceoryx2. Its compile-time example is a hypothetical `glibc_malloc_probe` using glibc-only APIs. Our actual and only case is different in kind: a **third-party dependency** that will not build on musl. That is what forces the `iceoryx` Cargo feature, the optional-dependency plumbing, and the target-gated-dependency question, none of which appear in the note. Working from the trait snippet alone, it could not have known.

Also unverified: "zcr-mpsc benches are allocation-free by design" is asserted about our code without having read it. Might well be true, but given the registry claim, I would confirm before relying on it. And if we do the allocator variant, prefer mimalloc over jemalloc: jemalloc's musl support is historically poor, which would defeat the purpose.

## The merge

Keep from the note: `TARGET_LIBC`, triple plus libc plus glibc version stamped into the report and the -3 record, skip-not-drop, the two-mechanism split, the build matrix across both arches, the allocator caveat and its variant.

Change: the declaration moves off the `Bench` trait and into the registry entry as data, so it survives being cfg'd out.

```rust
pub struct BenchEntry {
    pub name: &'static str,
    pub libc: LibcSupport,   // target-invariant: where it is meaningful
    pub run: Option<RunFn>,  // target-dependent: whether it is in this build
}
```

Add: the `iceoryx` feature and the optional-dependency question.

And the note actually forces a correction to something I said. I proposed the honesty test as `libc.allows(TARGET_LIBC) == run.is_some()`. With the two-mechanism split that is too strong, because "compiles but is not meaningful" is a legitimate state where `run` is `Some` and `allows` is false. The right invariant is one-directional:

> if `libc.allows(TARGET_LIBC)` then `run.is_some()`

Declared meaningful here but not compiled in is a bug. Compiled in but not meaningful is a runtime skip. That is a better test than mine, and it exists because of the note's distinction.

## One process point

The note is worth keeping, but it should get a correction pass before it sits in `notes/` as the design, since the `Box<dyn Bench>` premise and the missing iceoryx2 context will read as authority to whoever opens it next. That is the same rot problem your 2026-08-04 dogfood entry logged about doc links.

**The plain version:** web-claude got the principles right and gave us two things I had missed, the compile-versus-meaningful split and the allocator remedy. But it was working from the trait alone, so it assumed benches are registered as boxed trait objects, and they are not, they are plain function pointers. That matters because its mechanism asks a bench instance a question, and on musl the iceoryx benches do not exist to be asked. Move the declaration into the registry table as data and the two designs merge cleanly, with its split making the correctness test sharper than the one I proposed.

Want me to write up the merged design as a rung spec, and fix the note in place, or leave the note as the received artifact and put the merged version somewhere new?

3	Conventions the bot follows when reading and writing notes files (`TODO.md`,
4	`notes/todo-backlog.md`, `notes/bugs.md`, `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`, `notes/done.md`). One
5	source of truth lives here; [`notes/README.md`](../notes/README.md) points back. Read this
6	before editing a notes file.
7	
8	Universal file, pinned to the template repository; do not edit here. Project overrides go in
9	[custom.md](../custom.md).
10	
11	## File reads: read the slice you need
12	
13	Long notes files are appended to over time. Read only the slice your task needs; grep or read
14	further on demand.
15	
16	- **`TODO.md`** (the routine acquaint read): the first ~60 lines covers intro + `## In
17	  Progress` + the top of the ranked `## Todo` (priorities, #1 highest). `Read` with
18	  `offset=0, limit=60`. `## Ideas` sits below `## Todo`; read further only when chasing a
19	  lower-ranked entry, an Idea, a `[N]` ref, or auditing the whole list.
20	- **`notes/todo-backlog.md`**: the long-tail backlog (lower-priority entries below the ranked
21	  `## Todo`). Read only when picking up a backlog item; grep to locate it first.
22	- **`notes/bugs.md`**: the bug list. Small; read whole when triaging a bug or chasing the
23	  `## Bugs` pointer in TODO.md.
24	- **`notes/done.md`** + **`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`**: historical / append-mostly. Scan
25	  headings first (`grep '^## ' notes/chores/chores-NN.md`), then read only the section you
26	  need.
27	
28	**Why:** the routine read should stay small. `TODO.md` grows every cycle, so the backlog and
29	bugs live in files under `notes/` rather than inline; the same "slice you need" rule applies
30	to historical files.
31	
32	## Notes references
33	
34	Reference *citations* are double-bracketed so the brackets render: `[[N]]`, or `[[2]],[[3]]`
35	for several (comma-separated, not `[2,3]` or `[[2]][[3]]`). The `[N]:` definitions in a file's
36	`# References` section and inline `[text](url)` / `[text](#anchor)` links stay
37	single-bracketed.
38	
39	## Reference numbering
40	
41	Every note file (`TODO.md`, `todo-backlog.md`, `bugs.md`, `chores-NN.md`, `done.md`) keeps a
42	file-local `# References` section at the bottom. Reference numbers are scoped to that file:
43	`[1]` in `chores-07.md` and `[1]` in `chores-01.md` are independent slots that may point at
44	completely different URLs. New chores files start their numbering at `[1]`.
45	
46	Treat `[N]` like a **footnote**: the number is a local slot, only meaningful within its file's
47	`# References`. So a `[N]` *citation* (bare `[N]`, or doubled `[[N]]`) never reuses another
48	file's number; to cite a target a sibling file references, pick your own next-local slot and
49	define it (the same target may carry a different number in each file). A `[N]` *inside a code
50	span* (`` `[72]` ``) is different: that's a quoted identifier, literal text naming a ref-key
51	(often from another file's namespace), data, not a citation; it needs no definition here. To
52	point at a section of another file from prose, use an inline link with an anchor,
53	`[that section](../chores-07.md#...)`, not a bare number.
54	
55	A `chores-NN.md` `# References` entry is usually a `/notes/<file>.md#anchor` (or
56	`/ARCHITECTURE.md`) path, but may also be a **commit reference**,
57	`[N]: <commit-url-with-12-hex-SHA> "<full-40-hex-SHA>"`, cited by a rung of a section's
58	as-built ladder. See [Chores commit references](#chores-commit-references) for the why and the
59	exact shape.
60	
61	A file's `# References` can be **re-packed** to a contiguous `[1]..[N]` in
62	first-citation-appearance order: walk the file's prose in document order (`TODO.md`: `## Todo`
63	then `## Done`; `chores-NN.md`: top to bottom) and number refs as their first `[[N]]` citation
64	appears. This is a file-local rewrite, so only that file's `[[N]]` citations and `[N]:`
65	definitions move; every target and sibling file is untouched. A `[[N]]` inside a `` ` `` code
66	span is a literal token, not a citation, and is left alone. Do it opportunistically (when the
67	namespace has drifted enough to annoy), not on a schedule: `TODO.md` fragments fastest (entries
68	land and get pruned every cycle) and is the usual candidate; `chores-NN.md` / `done.md` are
69	append-mostly and only need it after an unusual event (e.g. a bulk retrofit that allocated
70	slots out of document order).
71	
72	## Markdown anchor links
73	
74	GitHub anchor algorithm: lowercase, strip non-alphanumeric characters in place, map remaining
75	spaces to hyphens 1-for-1. Do **not** collapse adjacent whitespace, so `a + b` -> `a--b`
76	(spaces on both sides of `+`), but `a: b` -> `a-b` (only trailing space on `:`). General
77	markdown reference: [markdownguide.org](https://www.markdownguide.org). GitHub publishes no
78	official spec for auto-generated anchors; the de-facto reference implementation is
79	[github-slugger](https://github.com/Flet/github-slugger).
80	
81	## Todo format
82	
83	`TODO.md` is organized into `## In Progress`, `## Todo` (strict priority rank, #1 highest;
84	long-tail backlog in [todo-backlog.md](../notes/todo-backlog.md)), `## Ideas`, `## Bugs`
85	(pointer to [bugs.md](../notes/bugs.md)), and `## Done` sections. Each item is a short
86	description with reference links to more detail.
87	
88	`## Todo` and `## Bugs` entries carry explicit `1.` `2.` ... numbers in the source. For
89	`## Todo` the number is its **priority rank** (#1 highest, descending); for `## Bugs` it's just
90	an index. They're for grepping and at-a-glance "let's do #1", **not stable IDs**: reorder (to
91	reprioritize), insert, or delete freely, then `vc-x1 fix-todo --no-dry-run` renumbers and
92	normalizes continuation-line indent, so any given number is positional. **To refer to a Todo
93	durably, name it by its title, a plain, greppable text mention.** Not its number (positional,
94	renumbered) and not a markdown link: a numbered list item has no anchor to link to.
95	
96	Numbering helps a human orient in a long list but makes links difficult and fragile, especially
97	an external reference pointing in, which can't be auto-fixed when the list renumbers. A robust
98	fix (a number-free anchor, or a number-tolerant dereference that matches the title slug and
99	wildcards the numeric prefix, since a GitHub slug like `5-foo` is encoded, not opaque, so the
100	title is recoverable) is a `validate-numbering` design question, out of scope here.
101	
102	`vc-x1 fix-todo` alone only previews; `vc-x1 validate-todo` is the read-only check. The
103	`## Done` section keeps `-` bullets, since items aren't referenced by number once completed.
104	
105	Example shape:
106	
107	```
108	# Todo
109	1. Add new feature X [details](features.md#feature-x)
110	2. Fix bug Y [[1]]
111	
112	# Done
113	- Fixed issue Z [[2]],[[3]]
114	
115	[1]: bugs.md#bug-y
116	[2]: issues.md#issue-z
117	[3]: fixes.md#fix-z
118	```
119	
120	## Retiring Done entries
121	
122	`TODO.md`'s `## Done` section is a rolling buffer of recently shipped work, not a permanent
123	log. Move entries into `done.md` at two natural beats:
124	
125	- **Closing a ladder**: when the final `X.Y.Z` (no suffix) commit ships, decide which prior
126	  entries are no longer needed for nearby context and migrate them.
127	- **Opening a new ladder**: at `X.Y.Z-0`, do the same sweep before bumping the
128	  version-of-record.
129	
130	Migration mechanics:
131	
132	- Move the bullet itself from `TODO.md > ## Done` to `done.md` (preserving the original ref
133	  number).
134	- Copy any references the moved entries cite into `done.md`'s `# References` section (those
135	  refs are file-local, so coexisting with `TODO.md`'s namespace is fine).
136	- Prune any references in `TODO.md > # References` no longer cited by anything in
137	  `## In Progress` / `## Todo` / `## Done`. This frees the numbers for future reuse.
138	
139	## Chores conventions
140	
141	### Headings and entries that record a commit
142	
143	A commit's title is reused verbatim across its records; see
144	[Conventional-commit shape](prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) for the
145	rule. Beyond the chores `##` header, that same string is used for the matching
146	`TODO.md > ## Done` entry and any `[N]` reference to that section. Titles carry **no
147	`(<version>)` suffix**; see
148	[Commit description](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#commit-description) for why. E.g. the chores
149	header `## refactor: extract config loader` and the Done line
150	`- refactor: extract config loader [[3]]`. The `## Done` entry uses the close-out commit's
151	title.
152	
153	This does **not** apply to organizational headings (`## Todo`, `## In Progress`,
154	`# References`) or to design `###` subsections inside a chores section; those are named for
155	whatever fits. Among the commit-recording ones, exact match is the strong default (nothing
156	absolute): a near-miss just makes it harder to line a record up with its commit.
157	
158	A commit-recording header is provisional while the work is in progress; the *last* edit before
159	`vc-x1 push` syncs it, and the `## Done` entry / `[N]` anchor for that commit, to the final
160	commit title. See [Markdown anchor links](#markdown-anchor-links) for the slug algorithm; the
161	pre-commit checklist catches a dangling `#anchor`, and a future `vc-x1 validate-repo` should
162	too (and should verify the recorded title matches the commit).
163	
164	Any pre-existing sections and `## Done` entries that predate this convention keep their
165	free-form text; the convention applies going forward.
166	
167	### Chores section content: no edit list; git is the record
168	
169	A chores section is: the as-built ladder (first content under the header; see below), then
170	[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) (intro + bullets) for what landed and why, and any `###`
171	design subsections. Bullets here are **conceptual** (design points, structural notes), never a
172	per-file edit list. That lives in the commit message body, which is the source of truth for
173	"what changed mechanically" (immutable, `git show`-able, naturally scoped to the commit). The
174	chores section is the source of truth for the design thinking; the two cross-link, neither
175	restates the other.
176	
177	The section is **built up per commit**: each work commit appends its own rung to the as-built
178	ladder + any narrative as it lands, rather than the narrative waiting for close-out (which only
179	*finalizes*: header title sync, design subsections). Full when-in-the-cycle timing lives in
180	cycle-protocol.md [Chores sections](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections); this note is
181	the pointer, so the two don't drift.
182	
183	When the intro starts wanting to explain a mechanism, hypothesis, or wrinkle, don't inflate it;
184	promote that to its own `###` subsection inside the same `chores-NN.md`. If the wrinkle is a
185	live design concern (something that *should* change, not just be recorded), also add a
186	`TODO.md` item with a `[N]` ref pointing at that subsection (todo->chores is the normal ref
187	direction).
188	
189	**Why:** a chores edit list and the commit body were specified to be the same content in two
190	places, and detail written twice drifts. Git owns the mechanical record; chores owns the
191	narrative; the ladder's commit refs link them.
192	
193	### Chores commit references
194	
195	The first content under a chores section header is the **as-built ladder**: one rung per
196	commit the section records, in landing order, each rung carrying its own `[N]` citation slot.
197	The same form is used for every cycle, single- or multi-commit; a single-commit cycle is a
198	one-rung ladder whose rung is the bare `X.Y.Z` close-out:
199	
200	```
201	## refactor: extract config loader
202	
203	- [[2]] 0.42.0-1 refactor: split loader from parser
204	- [[N]] 0.42.0 refactor: extract config loader
205	
206	<intro paragraph...>
207	```
208	
209	- The rung form is `- [[N]] X.Y.Z[-n] <title>`, with no `(current)` / `(done)` markers:
210	  as-built implies done (the in-flight markers live in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`).
211	- A rung is written with the literal `[[N]]` placeholder and backfilled in place with a real
212	  file-local slot once its commit's SHA is permanent (see Timing below).
213	- Rung citations use the file-local `[N]` reference machinery (see
214	  [Reference numbering](#reference-numbering)), **double-bracketed** so the brackets render.
215	  (`[[3]]` shows as a literal `[`, the `[3]` link, then a literal `]`; the inner `[3]`
216	  resolves against its `[3]:` definition, and CommonMark / GitHub / VS Code all do this.) The
217	  `# References` definition puts the **commit URL** as the destination, with the **full
218	  40-hex SHA** in the title slot:
219	
220	```
221	[3]: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/commit/<12-hex> "<40-hex>"
222	```
223	
224	- The 12-hex short SHA in the URL keeps it short; GitHub / GitLab resolve a unique prefix to
225	  the canonical commit page (GitLab's path has a `/-/` before `commit/`).
226	- The full SHA in the title is host-agnostic and unambiguous: it survives a repo host change,
227	  `git show <40-hex>` works in any clone, and external tooling scraping the notes (a database,
228	  say) gets the canonical identifier.
229	
230	**Timing.** A commit's SHA isn't stable until it lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a
231	long-lived release/patch branch), because a rebase or squash rewrites it on the way. A commit
232	can't record its own SHA, so the fill lands one push later: every rung opens with the literal
233	`[[N]]` placeholder, and each push backfills the rungs of the commits the previous push made
234	permanent. On a topic branch a section waits until the branch lands. The commit itself is the
235	record, and `git log --grep "<title>"` finds it. See cycle-protocol
236	[Commits backfill](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill).
237	
238	Sections that predate this convention keep their `Commits:` lines; the ladder form applies
239	going forward.
240	
241	### Chores file Table of Contents
242	
243	Each `chores-NN.md` carries a `## Table of Contents` section between the file intro and the
244	first commit-recording section: one `- [<title>](#<anchor>)` entry per commit-recording `##`
245	section, in file order.
246	
247	- Entries are title-only, with no version and no `[N]` refs, so the TOC never needs backfill:
248	  the TOC navigates, the section's as-built ladder records.
249	- Append the entry when the section opens; the entry text participates in the same last-edit
250	  title sync as the section header and the `## Done` entry.
251	- Design `###` subsections stay out of the TOC.
252	- Files predating the convention gain a TOC opportunistically, not on a schedule.

### Chores section content: no edit list; git is the record

A chores section is: the as-built ladder (first content under the header; see below), then
[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) (intro + bullets) for what landed and why, and any `###`
design subsections. Bullets here are **conceptual** (design points, structural notes), never a
per-file edit list. That lives in the commit message body, which is the source of truth for
"what changed mechanically" (immutable, `git show`-able, naturally scoped to the commit). The
chores section is the source of truth for the design thinking; the two cross-link, neither
restates the other.

The section is **built up per commit**: each work commit appends its own rung to the as-built
ladder + any narrative as it lands, rather than the narrative waiting for close-out (which only
*finalizes*: header title sync, design subsections). Full when-in-the-cycle timing lives in
cycle-protocol.md [Chores sections](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections); this note is
the pointer, so the two don't drift.

When the intro starts wanting to explain a mechanism, hypothesis, or wrinkle, don't inflate it;
promote that to its own `###` subsection inside the same `chores-NN.md`. If the wrinkle is a
live design concern (something that *should* change, not just be recorded), also add a
`TODO.md` item with a `[N]` ref pointing at that subsection (todo->chores is the normal ref
direction).

**Why:** a chores edit list and the commit body were specified to be the same content in two
places, and detail written twice drifts. Git owns the mechanical record; chores owns the
narrative; the ladder's commit refs link them.

### Chores commit references

The first content under a chores section header is the **as-built ladder**: one rung per
commit the section records, in landing order, each rung carrying its own `[N]` citation slot.
The same form is used for every cycle, single- or multi-commit; a single-commit cycle is a
one-rung ladder whose rung is the bare `X.Y.Z` close-out:

```
## refactor: extract config loader

- [[2]] 0.42.0-1 refactor: split loader from parser
- [[N]] 0.42.0 refactor: extract config loader

<intro paragraph...>
```

- The rung form is `- [[N]] X.Y.Z[-n] <title>`, with no `(current)` / `(done)` markers:
  as-built implies done (the in-flight markers live in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`).
- A rung is written with the literal `[[N]]` placeholder and backfilled in place with a real
  file-local slot once its commit's SHA is permanent (see Timing below).
- Rung citations use the file-local `[N]` reference machinery (see
  [Reference numbering](#reference-numbering)), **double-bracketed** so the brackets render.
  (`[[3]]` shows as a literal `[`, the `[3]` link, then a literal `]`; the inner `[3]`
  resolves against its `[3]:` definition, and CommonMark / GitHub / VS Code all do this.) The
  `# References` definition puts the **commit URL** as the destination, with the **full
  40-hex SHA** in the title slot:

```
[3]: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/commit/<12-hex> "<40-hex>"
```

- The 12-hex short SHA in the URL keeps it short; GitHub / GitLab resolve a unique prefix to
  the canonical commit page (GitLab's path has a `/-/` before `commit/`).
- The full SHA in the title is host-agnostic and unambiguous: it survives a repo host change,
  `git show <40-hex>` works in any clone, and external tooling scraping the notes (a database,
  say) gets the canonical identifier.

**Timing.** A commit's SHA isn't stable until it lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a
long-lived release/patch branch), because a rebase or squash rewrites it on the way. A commit
can't record its own SHA, so the fill lands one push later: every rung opens with the literal
`[[N]]` placeholder, and each push backfills the rungs of the commits the previous push made
permanent. On a topic branch a section waits until the branch lands. The commit itself is the
record, and `git log --grep "<title>"` finds it. See cycle-protocol
[Commits backfill](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill).

Sections that predate this convention keep their `Commits:` lines; the ladder form applies
going forward.

### Chores file Table of Contents

Each `chores-NN.md` carries a `## Table of Contents` section between the file intro and the
first commit-recording section: one `- [<title>](#<anchor>)` entry per commit-recording `##`
section, in file order.

- Entries are title-only, with no version and no `[N]` refs, so the TOC never needs backfill:
  the TOC navigates, the section's as-built ladder records.
- Append the entry when the section opens; the entry text participates in the same last-edit
  title sync as the section header and the `## Done` entry.
- Design `###` subsections stay out of the TOC.
- Files predating the convention gain a TOC opportunistically, not on a schedule.

232	## Todo
233	
234	Entries are in **strict priority rank**, #1 highest, descending. Reprioritize by moving an
235	entry, then `vc-x1 fix-todo --no-dry-run TODO.md` to renumber. The numbers are positional rank,
236	not stable IDs. To refer to a Todo, name it by its **title** (a greppable mention; a numbered
237	list item has no anchor to link to), not its number. Long-tail entries live in
238	[todo-backlog.md](notes/todo-backlog.md). Use the
239	[Prose Form in AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md#prose-form); deeper detail goes in
240	`notes/chores/chores-NN.md` design subsections (link via `[N]` ref).
241	
242	1. Report interpretation guide: a reader-oriented "how to read a report" walkthrough in README,
243	   teaching what each surface means and, above all, what to conclude from it
244	   - surfaces to cover:
245	     - the band table: first/last/range/count/mean per quantile band
246	     - the summary rows: mean/stdev, the trimmed row, blocks mean/CI95/LSC
247	     - the grade block: env warmup/bench vs run rows, per-signal letters, the settle cell
248	     - the -v warmup table and its exit/window/clock summary line
249	   - lead with worked examples, the 2026-08-02 3900X trio (plain -d 5, --blocks 100,
250	     --blocks 1000):
251	     - duty cycle selects the bistable state: sustained load climbs into the fast state
252	       (~21.8 ns), while 5 ms bursts between 1-10 ms sleeps hold the slow state (24.0 ns)
253	     - grade A certifies internal consistency of the state the run held, not a canonical number
254	     - so A/B wants matched duty cycle; --blocks 1000 read CI95 0.0 ns unpinned by holding one
255	       state for 13 s
256	   - the report is dense by design; the guide is the decoder the grade-block compaction (0.23.2)
257	     assumed exists
258	2. Interleaved multi-arm comparison: take a list of benches as *arms* of one comparison and rank
259	   them, which is what the harness is actually for (raised 2026-08-04; ranked here on arrival,
260	   move it up if it should lead)
261	   - **sequenced after the measure-reproducibility rerun, deliberately.** Every open design
262	     question below is one that rerun's records answer: which estimator has the smallest
263	     run-to-run scatter, whether re-exec matters or in-process rounds dominate, and how big each
264	     box's drift floor is. Building first means guessing all three and rebuilding
265	   - the vocabulary it needs, added when the code does and not before: an **arm** is one thing
266	     being compared (a bench, or a bench plus pin plus config), a **round** is one pass over all
267	     arms. Each level of the existing hierarchy earns its name by what it re-randomizes: a block
268	     re-rolls short-term scheduling noise, a fresh process re-rolls ASLR / allocator / page
269	     mapping / thread placement, separation in time re-rolls thermal and P-state history, a
270	     reboot re-rolls everything
271	   - interleave, never concatenate: A-then-B confounds the difference with drift, while
272	     alternating makes every shared factor common-mode so it cancels in the paired difference.
273	     Counterbalance the order (ABBA, rotating with three or more arms) so linear drift cancels
274	     rather than aliasing onto the result
275	   - the cost interleaving buys, and it must be stated in the report: both arms are resident at

Continuation of [chores-05](chores-05.md). Records landed work; conventions in
[agent-data/notes.md](../../agent-data/notes.md#chores-conventions) and
[cycle-protocol.md](../cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections).

## Table of Contents

- [feat: dynamic warmup](#feat-dynamic-warmup)
- [feat: measure reproducibility](#feat-measure-reproducibility)

## feat: dynamic warmup

- [[N]] 0.24.0-0 feat: dynamic warmup opening
- [[N]] 0.24.0-1 refactor: one parameterized warm loop
- [[N]] 0.24.0-2 feat: warm until the trailing window grades A
- [[N]] 0.24.0-3 feat: warm where the bench runs

job rather than a cross-module one. Left alone here, since this rung adds nothing.

The move also flushed out the doc links, which `cargo doc` had been quietly warning about: 6
unresolved before it, 18 during, 0 after. Twelve were the move's own and were fixed by
qualifying the path. The 6 that predate it were a mix: `BURST_TOL` and `EnvGrade` cited from
inside `gauge.rs`'s nested threshold module and needed `super::`; `BATCH_FLOOR_Q` was private, so
it is `pub(crate)` now that a sibling module's docs cite it; `TProbe::record` needed its full
path from a bench; `MICRO_PROBE_GROUP` was a rename casualty and is `PROBE_GROUP_PAIRS`; and
`ENV_PROBES` no longer exists at all, so the sentence citing it now states the reasoning without
inventing a current probe count. One `<time>` in a doc comment was also parsing as an HTML tag,
and is a code span now.

The acceptance test moved behind an `acceptance` feature in the same rung. It had been
`#[ignore]`d, which meant it announced itself in every `cargo test` while never checking
anything; `required-features` on the test target removes it from the default build instead.
`clippy` gained `--all-features` so the gated target does not slip out of the lint sweep, and
the invocation is recorded in custom.md as an acceptance check rather than validation, since it
grades the box and not the code.
